mcqs.question: A screen keeps `useQuery({ queryKey: ['inbox'], queryFn: fetchInbox, gcTime: 10 * 60_000 })` and leaves `staleTime` untouched. Which pair of outcomes actually follows?
options: The inbox stops refetching for ten minutes, and the entry stays in memory for ten minutes after the screen unmounts.

The inbox still refetches on mount, window focus and reconnect because the data is stale as soon as it arrives; the ten minutes only start once the last observer unmounts, and the entry is discarded after that.
The ten minutes run from the moment the entry was created, so a long-lived screen can lose its data mid-session while it is still mounted.
A remount inside the ten minutes renders `isPending` with no data until the background refetch lands, because the entry is retained but not servable.
mcqs.explanation: `gcTime` is a retention policy: it counts from the moment the entry has no mounted observer and it never gates a request, so it cannot stop the default refetches while `staleTime` sits at `0` and mount, focus and reconnect all treat the data as stale (https://tanstack.com/query/latest/docs/framework/react/guides/important-defaults). Freshness is the other knob: only raising `staleTime` or invalidating on purpose changes those triggers. The strongest distractor is the first one, and it is the exact mix-up the two names invite — people raise `gcTime` when they mean `staleTime`, see no drop in refetches, and conclude the library is broken. Option 3 fails because the collection clock starts at zero observers, not at creation: a mounted query is never collected, however long it lives. Option 4 confuses 'stale' with 'absent': a retained entry renders immediately and refetches in the background (`isFetching`, not `isPending`), and `isPending` means there is no data at all.

mcqs.question: A screen runs `useQuery({ queryKey: ['orders', { status }], queryFn: () => fetchOrders({ tenantId, status }) })`. Switching workspace keeps the same `status`, the rows stay on the previous tenant's orders, the network tab shows no request on some switches, and a reload fixes it. What is the defect, and which key fixes it?
options: The key's object literal is recreated on every render, so the entry is missed each time; hoist it into a `useMemo` so its identity is stable.
`tenantId` changes the request but is absent from the key, so the observer keeps reading the same entry and no request is fired; it belongs in the key as `['orders', { tenantId, status }]`.
Nothing is wrong with the identity, the data is simply fresh; set `staleTime: 0` so a tenant change always re-requests.
The entry has to be scoped per session, so include the auth token in the key: `['orders', token, { status }]`.
mcqs.explanation: The key is the cache identity and every input the query function sends has to appear in it; with `tenantId` missing, the switch does not change the observer's key, so there is no new entry to fetch and no automatic refetch, because a prop change is not a mount (https://tanstack.com/query/latest/docs/framework/react/guides/query-keys). The strongest distractor is the `useMemo` one, because it imports a real rule from other libraries: here the default `queryKeyHashFn` hashes structurally, so a fresh literal with the same content is the same key and memoising it changes nothing — the missing input is the defect, not an unstable identity. Option 3 changes nothing in place (the switch fires no trigger), and when a mount or focus does refetch it refills the same shared entry, so switching back can serve the other tenant's rows; two tenants open at once still collide. Option 4 puts a rotating secret into keys that devtools and logs show, and busts the entry on every token refresh; scope by tenant id instead.

mcqs.question: Three endpoints are declared: `getPosts` provides the general `'Post'` tag, `getPost(id)` provides `{ type: 'Post', id }`, and `editPost` invalidates `{ type: 'Post', id }` with the edited id. After editing post 7, the detail page for 7 refetches and the list keeps the old title. Which queries were invalidated, and why?
options: Both: the list's result contains post 7, so any query whose data includes the edited entity is invalidated.
Only the queries that provide `{ type: 'Post', id: 7 }` — matching runs over declared tags, not over the contents of a result, and the list declared only the general `'Post'` tag.
Both: a specific tag is a subset of its type, so invalidating `{ type: 'Post', id: 7 }` also matches the general `'Post'` tag.
Neither until the next mount: invalidation only marks entries, and the refetch happens when a component subscribes again.
mcqs.explanation: Tags are labels an endpoint declares and invalidation compares the invalidated tag against those declarations, so a query that provided only `'Post'` is untouched by `{ type: 'Post', id: 7 }` (https://redux-toolkit.js.org/rtk-query/usage/automated-refetching). The matching is deliberately asymmetric: type-wide invalidation does match every specific id, the reverse does not. The strongest distractor is the first one, because it reasons about content — 'the list shows post 7, so it must be stale' — and that is exactly the intuition the tag system refuses: RTK Query keeps no normalized store, so a cached copy only learns about a change through a tag it declared. The fix is the list providing `{ type: 'Post', id }` for each row it renders (plus an abstract `'LIST'` id if creates and deletes also need it). Option 3 inverts the subsumption, and option 4 gets the timing wrong: subscribed entries refetch on fulfilment, which is why the detail page updated at all.

mcqs.question: An optimistic add follows the usual shape: `onMutate` snapshots with `getQueryData`, writes with `setQueryData` and returns the snapshot; `onError` restores it; `onSettled` invalidates. In production the new row appears, then vanishes for a moment while the list shows the pre-add state, then comes back after the mutation settles. Which change addresses the root cause?
options: Start `onMutate` with `await client.cancelQueries({ queryKey: ['todos'] })` so a refetch that was already in flight cannot resolve on top of the prediction.
Set `staleTime: Infinity` on the todos query so it does not refetch while the mutation is pending.
Move the `invalidateQueries` call from `onSettled` into `onMutate` so the server response is the last thing to land.
Wrap the `setQueryData` call in `queueMicrotask` or `setTimeout(0)` so it runs after any pending refetch promise.
mcqs.explanation: The vanished row is a race, not a render bug: a refetch that started before the write resolves after it and replaces the predicted list with pre-mutation server data, and the settlement invalidation then fetches it back — hence appear, vanish, return. Cancelling the affected queries is the documented first step precisely because it reverts in-flight work for those keys (https://tanstack.com/query/latest/docs/framework/react/guides/optimistic-updates). The strongest distractor is `staleTime: Infinity`, the 'just stop refetching' reflex: `staleTime` decides which triggers start a request, so it cannot recall one already on the wire, and it also blocks the reconciliation refetch that keeps the cache honest. Moving the invalidation earlier reads the pre-mutation state before the command even runs and trades a rollback window for it, and deferring the write only reorders two things that must not race, since timer and network completion order is not guaranteed.

mcqs.question: `useGetPostQuery(1)` is mounted in a sidebar and in a detail panel. The panel unmounts at 10 s, the sidebar at 30 s, and `keepUnusedDataFor` is left at its default. At 75 s a route mounts `useGetPostQuery(1)` again, and at 6 minutes another one does. What happens?
options: Both mounts issue a request: RTK Query has no `staleTime`, so every mount of an endpoint fetches.

Both mounts join the same reference-counted entry; the count reaches zero at 30 s and the 60 s grace expires around 90 s, so the 75 s mount is served from cache with no request and the 6-minute mount is a cold load with `isLoading`.
The entry is deleted when the detail panel unmounts at 10 s, so both later mounts fetch.
The entry is never collected while the API slice is registered; `keepUnusedDataFor` only decides whether the cached data counts as fresh.
mcqs.explanation: Identity is endpoint plus serialized arguments and the entry is reference-counted: while any subscriber is mounted the clock does not run, and once the count hits zero the entry survives `keepUnusedDataFor` seconds — 60 by default — before removal (https://redux-toolkit.js.org/rtk-query/usage/cache-behavior). The strongest distractor is the first one: 'no `staleTime`' does not mean 'always request', because `refetchOnMountOrArgChange`, `refetchOnFocus` and `refetchOnReconnect` are all off by default, so a cached entry is served with no request even when the data is hours old. Option 3 stops counting at the first unmount and ignores the second subscriber. Option 4 is the `keepUnusedDataFor`-as-`staleTime` conflation: RTK Query has no freshness concept at all, so retention has nothing to imitate; it only controls how long the bytes live.

mcqs.question: A mutation declares `invalidatesTags: ['Post']` while twenty post detail pages are open, each providing `{ type: 'Post', id }`. What does that type-wide tag do when the mutation fulfils?
options: It matches only endpoints that declared the general `'Post'` tag; specific id tags live in a separate namespace.
It matches every provided Post tag of that type, specific ids included, so all twenty subscribed detail pages refetch — which is why type-wide invalidation is the expensive option.
It removes the twenty entries from the store without requests, so the pages render empty until they are remounted.
It invalidates nothing until each page is remounted, because invalidation is evaluated per subscription at mount time.
mcqs.explanation: A general invalidation matches all provided tags of that type — `'Post'`, `{ type: 'Post' }` and every `{ type: 'Post', id }` — and each subscribed match refetches in the background (https://redux-toolkit.js.org/rtk-query/usage/automated-refetching). It is the mirror image of the specific case, where only the same id matches, and that is why the sledgehammer is the wrong default once many details are open. The strongest distractor is the namespace one, because the opposite asymmetry makes it sound consistent: invalidating a specific id does leave a general-only provider untouched, so people assume the general tag likewise spares specific ones. Option 3 describes removal, which only happens to unsubscribed entries; these twenty pages are mounted, so they refetch. Option 4 inverts the lifecycle — tag matches are resolved when the mutation fulfils, not when a component mounts.

mcqs.question: A cursor-paginated list built with `useInfiniteQuery` ships a "Load more" button and also fires `fetchNextPage` from a scroll handler. Operators report duplicate rows at page boundaries and pages that sometimes shrink after an invalidation refetch. Which change matches the documented behaviour of infinite queries?
options: Raise `staleTime` so cached pages are not refetched while the next page is loading
Guard `fetchNextPage` while a page fetch is in flight (for example `!isFetching`) and, defensively, deduplicate merged pages by stable item id while preserving server order
Switch to numbered offset pagination so page boundaries become deterministic
Set `gcTime: 0` so the shared entry is rebuilt from scratch on every page
mcqs.explanation: One infinite query is one shared cache entry holding `pages` and `pageParams`, so two overlapping `fetchNextPage` calls can write over each other; the guard keeps a single page fetch in flight, and merging by stable id keeps an API that repeats a row at a boundary from rendering it twice (https://tanstack.com/query/latest/docs/framework/react/guides/infinite-queries). The strongest distractor is the offset switch: offsets are only deterministic over a frozen snapshot, so an insert or delete between requests shifts every later row and page 2 replays rows already shown on page 1 — the exact duplicate this option claims to remove. `staleTime` governs refetch freshness, not concurrent page fetches, and `gcTime: 0` throws away the pages you are paging through.

mcqs.question: A custom `loadResults(q)` helper already receives TanStack Query's `signal`, passes it to `fetch`, and logs an `AbortError` when the query becomes obsolete. Under which condition can the screen still commit a stale result?
options: Never: once the request is aborted the browser guarantees no response reaches your handlers
Only when `staleTime` was left at its default of `0`
When the response had already left the server or a proxy before the abort took effect, so the `then` callbacks still run and need a request-identity check before committing
Only when two different query keys are in play, because they share one cache entry
mcqs.explanation: Abort is best effort: an abort that fires after the response is already in flight does not un-resolve the promise, so the handler still runs and can overwrite newer state unless it compares a monotonically increasing request id before committing (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortController). Cancellation is a resource optimisation; the identity check is the correctness guard. The strongest distractor is "never": it treats `abort()` as a transactional guarantee, which is why reviewers accept code that aborts and then commits unconditionally. `staleTime` is a refetch policy, and different query keys are separate entries, so the last option inverts how identity works.

mcqs.question: A query function throws `new ApiError(response.status)` for any non-2xx response. The team wants a `401` to fail immediately with a user-visible recovery action while a `503` gets two more attempts. Which configuration expresses that policy?
options: Leave the default `retry: 3`; the library inspects HTTP status codes and skips client errors
`retry: (count, error) => error.status >= 500 && count < 2`, with the final error rendered by the screen's error state or error boundary
`retry: false` plus a `useEffect` that calls `refetch()` whenever `isError` becomes true
`retry: (count) => count < 2` with a fixed `retryDelay` of 30 seconds
mcqs.explanation: TanStack Query knows nothing about HTTP semantics: it retries whatever the query function throws, three times by default with capped exponential backoff, so the predicate is where a deterministic 4xx is excluded (https://tanstack.com/query/latest/docs/framework/react/guides/query-retries). Keeping the classification in the fetching layer and the recovery UI above it is the separation the policy needs. The strongest distractor is the default-retry option: it produces exactly the bug this policy exists to prevent — three useless attempts on an expired token plus a delayed, noisier error. `retry: false` with an effect moves policy into the component and refetches a revoked session forever, and the status-blind predicate still retries the 401.

mcqs.question: An RTK Query endpoint opens a WebSocket inside `onCacheEntryAdded` and applies every message with `updateCachedData`. Some events carry only `{ id, updatedAt }` instead of the full entity the query returns. What keeps the cache honest?
options: Upsert the partial message anyway; fields it omits simply keep their previous cached values

Treat the event as a change signal: when it does not carry the shape the query returns, invalidate the relevant tag (or refetch that id) instead of guessing, and apply ordering or version rules so an older event cannot overwrite newer data
Move the socket outside the cache lifecycle and mirror every message into a global store that becomes the source of truth
Close the socket when a component unmounts instead of waiting for `cacheEntryRemoved`
mcqs.explanation: A streamed event is a change signal, often partial; the cache holds the representation, so an event that lacks fields must trigger a refetch rather than invent them, and version/ordering checks stop a late event from regressing the row (https://redux-toolkit.js.org/rtk-query/usage/streaming-updates). The strongest distractor is the partial upsert: for a row already in the cache it silently keeps values the server may have changed, and for a row that belongs to another page it fabricates a half-populated entity — which then renders as valid data. A second store restores the two-sources-of-truth problem, and closing per component unmount leaks or duplicates sockets when two subscribers share one entry; cleanup belongs to `cacheEntryRemoved`.

scenarios.prompt: A workspace switcher sits above an orders table. Operators report that after switching from tenant A to tenant B the table still shows A's rows — sometimes for a few seconds, sometimes until a full reload — and that the network tab shows no request on some of those switches. Diagnose the cache identity, fix it, and state how you would prove the fix and what you want to happen on a tenant switch.
scenarios.modelAnswer:
**Diagnosis.** The key is the cache identity, and this one omits `tenantId` while `fetchOrders` sends it. A tenant switch changes a prop, not the key, so the observer stays on `['orders', { status, page }]`: no key change means no fetch, which is why some switches produce no request at all. The rows on screen are tenant A's because that entry is what the component is reading; a reload hides the bug by forcing a fresh mount with the new tenant. The seconds-long variant is the same entry being refilled by a trigger (mount or focus) while `tenantId` in the closure is already B — the request is correct, the identity is not, so A's entry and B's response meet briefly. With `staleTime > 0` the entry is not even stale, and that is the 'does not change until I reload' report.

**Why this is not just a UX bug.** Two tenants can be mounted at once — a side-by-side comparison, an embedded view — and both would write into one entry: whichever response lands last wins the whole screen. That is a data-exposure finding, not a cosmetic one, so it belongs in the ticket with that severity.

**Fix.** Put every response-affecting input in the key, from one place: `queryKeys.orders(filters)` returning `['orders', { tenantId, status, page }]`, used by the hook, by every `invalidateQueries` and by `setQueryData` in mutations. Plain serializable values only: object property order does not matter to the default hash, array order does, and the token does not belong there (scope by tenant id; a token rotates and would bust the cache for nothing).

**A tenant switch is a boundary, not a refetch.** Changing tenant invalidates everything derived from the old scope, including pages and widgets that are not on screen now; that is the legitimate use of `queryClient.clear()` or a per-root `removeQueries`, because a filter-scoped invalidation will always miss something. Any app state derived from the old tenant goes with it.

**What I would not do.** `enabled: false` until the tenant resolves delays the fetch but keeps the shared entry; `staleTime: 0` only makes the wrong entry refill more eagerly; a `key` prop on the component remounts the tree and throws away unrelated UI state.

**Proof.** Network tab: switch tenant and see exactly one request per visible key, carrying the new `tenantId`; switch back and see A's rows, from cache or after a request, never B's. Then add regression tests at the hook level — two different filters produce two entries, and two tenants rendered at once stay isolated.
rubric: Names the missing `tenantId` as a cache-identity defect and reads the no-request switch as the same entry being observed, not as a stale-refetch problem.
Rebuilds the key with every response-affecting input through a single key factory, and keeps secrets out of it.
Explains why `enabled`, `staleTime: 0` or a remount do not fix identity.
Treats the tenant switch as a cache boundary (clear or remove) and notes the cross-tenant exposure when two tenants are mounted.
States an observable acceptance check: one request with the new tenant on switch, no cross-tenant rows, concurrent tenants isolated.

scenarios.prompt: A reviewer approved this handler with 'we invalidate on error, so it self-heals'. Users report two things: the added row sometimes disappears on the next window focus and comes back later, and when the POST fails the row can sit there looking saved with no error anywhere. For each part of the handler, say what it actually does, then rewrite it so a failed mutation and an in-flight refetch cannot lose the pre-existing list.
rubric: Explains the blink as an uncancelled refetch resolving after the prediction, not as a rendering bug.
Distinguishes rollback (restore the snapshot) from reconciliation (invalidate) and states that invalidation alone leaves the row when the read-back also fails.
Implements async `onMutate` with cancellation, snapshot, predicted write using a temporary id, and returns the context.
Restores in `onError` and surfaces the failure to the user; invalidates in `onSettled` on both paths.
Names the overlap limit of a single snapshot and either the local-pending alternative or `scope` serialisation.

scenarios.prompt: Design review on a posts API. Two complaints: after creating a post the network tab shows the list refetching and every post detail page ever opened refetching, and after renaming a post the detail page updates while the list row keeps the old title. Explain what the current tags do, then redesign them so each write refetches exactly what it invalidated.
scenarios.modelAnswer:
**Both symptoms are the same asymmetry.** A type-wide invalidation matches every provided tag of that type, specific ids included, so `addPost`'s `'Post'` hits the list and every open detail page. A specific invalidation matches only the same id, so `editPost`'s `{ type: 'Post', id }` hits the detail page and leaves the list alone — the list declared only the general tag. Tags are matched against declarations, never against the contents of a result: the list obviously contains the renamed post, and it still does not care.

**The redesigned contract.** The list owns two labels: one per row it displays, and one abstract id for the collection.

```ts
getPosts: build.query<Post[], void>({
  query: () => 'posts',
  providesTags: (result = []) => [
    { type: 'Post', id: 'LIST' },
    ...result.map(({ id }) => ({ type: 'Post' as const, id })),
  ],
}),
addPost: build.mutation<Post, NewPost>({
  query: (body) => ({ url: 'posts', method: 'POST', body }),
  invalidatesTags: [{ type: 'Post', id: 'LIST' }],
}),
```

`addPost` now refetches the list (it provides `LIST`) and no detail page (they provide ids only). `editPost` keeps `{ type: 'Post', id }`, which now reaches the detail page and every list that provided that row tag — the rename shows up in both without a type-wide storm. A delete invalidates `LIST` plus the removed row id. `'LIST'` must not be a value a real id can take: safe with numeric ids, so use a prefix such as `'__list'` if ids are strings.

**Two mechanics worth stating out loud.** Invalidation fires when the mutation is fulfilled, not when it starts, so a rejected mutation invalidates nothing — that is why optimistic paths need their own cache writes. And the reaction depends on subscribers: mounted queries refetch in the background, unmounted entries are removed, so returning to a detail page after an edit is a cold load. That is `keepUnusedDataFor` behaviour, not a tag bug, and it is a product decision, not something the tags can fix.

**Smell test.** Creating a post should cost exactly one request: the list. If a write needs three or four invalidations to look consistent, the tag graph is shaped wrong, usually a collection that never declared which rows it shows.

**Verification.** After create: one list request, zero detail requests. After an edit of id 7: the detail for 7 plus every list that shows row 7. After a delete: the list, and no detail refetch for the removed id.
rubric: Reads type-wide invalidation as matching specific ids too and specific invalidation as matching only the same id — the asymmetry behind both symptoms.
Has the list provide a per-row item tag plus a non-colliding abstract collection id, and keeps detail queries on entity tags.
Scopes `addPost` to the collection tag and `editPost` to the entity tag, and says why the edit now reaches the list.
States when invalidation runs (on fulfilment) and how subscriber presence decides refetch versus removal.
Gives request-level acceptance criteria per operation, or names the tag-graph smell when a write needs many invalidations.

scenarios.prompt: This search component was approved because it "has the request-id guard". Two problems remain: one mounted instance can silently suppress another instance's results, and obsolete requests still consume bandwidth and parse work. Find both, explain why the guard as written is not enough, and rewrite the component.
rubric: Identifies the module-scope counter as a cross-instance bug and moves identity to per-observer state (ref) or to the query key.
Separates the two concerns: abort for wasted work, identity check before commit for correctness — and does not claim abort alone prevents a stale render.
Passes a signal through to `fetch` (from the query function or a per-run `AbortController`) and aborts in cleanup.
Checks `res.ok` and throws a classified error, and treats `AbortError` as a non-error that is neither rendered nor retried.
Places debounce as traffic shaping, and states that the final error surfaces to the screen's error state with a retry action.
